body.en: HL Topic 1 extends SL algebra with proof by induction and complex numbers — the foundation for much of higher mathematics.
Structure: (1) Base case: verify for \(n=1\) (or initial \(n\)). (2) Inductive hypothesis: assume true for \(n=k\). (3) Inductive step: prove true for \(n=k+1.\) (4) Conclude.

title.en: ⊙ Explorer · Complex numbers on the Argand plane

ariaLabel.en: A complex number z plotted as a point on the Argand plane, with its conjugate, modulus, and argument shown

caption.en: z, its conjugate, modulus, and argument

note.en: z = a + bi (indigo dot) and its conjugate z̄ = a − bi (amber, dashed segment) are mirror images across the real axis — exactly what negating the imaginary part does geometrically. |z| is the dot's distance from the origin; arg(z) is the angle the segment from the origin to z makes with the positive real axis, drawn as an arc. Drag a or b negative to move z into another quadrant and watch arg(z) jump to the correctly-adjusted value, not just arctan(b/a) taken literally.

label.en: ● Polar form and de Moivre's theorem

body.en:
\[z=r(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)=re^{i\theta}\quad(r=|z|,\;\theta=\arg z).\]\[z^n=r^n(\cos n\theta+i\sin n\theta)\quad(\text{de Moivre's theorem}).\]

\(n\)-th roots of unity: solutions to \(z^n=1\) are \(e^{2\pi ik/n}\) for \(k=0,1,\ldots,n-1.\)

title.en: ⊙ Explorer · De Moivre's theorem on the unit circle

ariaLabel.en: The unit circle with a point z at angle theta, its nth power at angle n-theta, and the n-th roots of unity marked

caption.en: The n-th roots of unity: angle and coordinates of each

ariaLabel.en: Modulus r of z, from 0.5 to 1.5

note.en: z = r·cis θ (indigo) and zⁿ = rⁿ·cis(nθ) (amber, dashed) — this is de Moivre's theorem in full: raising z to the nth power multiplies the angle by n AND raises the modulus to the nth power. The gray rings are the n-th roots of unity (always on the unit circle, r = 1), k = 0, …, n−1, evenly spaced 360°/n apart starting at angle 0°. Set r = 1 and drag θ to a multiple of that spacing to land zⁿ exactly on z = 1, the k = 0 root. Push r above or below 1 and watch zⁿ leave the unit circle — outward for r > 1, inward for r < 1 — since |zⁿ| = rⁿ grows or shrinks with n, unlike the roots of unity themselves.

body.en:
A system of up to three linear equations in three unknowns can be solved by elimination: combine pairs of equations to cancel one variable at a time, reducing to a smaller system, until a single equation in one unknown remains — then substitute back up.

Geometrically, each equation \(ax+by+cz=d\) is a plane in 3D (Chapter 3 of this track studies these directly). Solving the system asks how three planes intersect:

  • Unique solution — the three planes meet at exactly one point (the generic case).
  • No solution — elimination produces a contradiction like \(0=k\) for \(k\neq0\); geometrically, no point lies on all three planes at once (e.g. two are parallel, or the three form a triangular "tube" with no common point).
  • Infinitely many solutions — elimination produces an identity like \(0=0\), leaving a free parameter; geometrically, the planes share a common line (or are all the same plane).

label.en: Worked Example 1.4 — Solving a 3×3 system by elimination

solution.en:
Label the equations (1), (2), (3). Add (1) and (3) to eliminate \(z\): \((x+y+z)+(x+2y-z)=6+2\Rightarrow2x+3y=8\) — call this (4).

Subtract (2) from (1) to eliminate \(z\) again: \((x+y+z)-(2x-y+z)=6-3\Rightarrow-x+2y=3\Rightarrow x=2y-3\) — call this (5).

Substitute (5) into (4): \(2(2y-3)+3y=8\Rightarrow4y-6+3y=8\Rightarrow7y=14\Rightarrow y=2.\)

Then \(x=2(2)-3=1\), and from (1): \(1+2+z=6\Rightarrow z=3.\)

Check in (2): \(2(1)-2+3=3.\) ✓ Check in (3): \(1+2(2)-3=2.\) ✓

Solution: \((x,y,z)=(1,2,3)\) — the unique point where all three planes meet.

problem.en: Write \(z=1+i\sqrt{3}\) in polar form and find \(z^6.\)

body.en:
Express \(z=-1+i\sqrt{3}\) in polar form and find \(z^6.\)

Show solution

\(r=2,\quad\theta=\frac{2\pi}{3}.\quad z=2e^{i2\pi/3}.\)

\(z^6=2^6e^{i4\pi}=64(\cos4\pi+i\sin4\pi)=64.\)

Prove \(\sum_{r=1}^n r = \dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}\) by induction.

Solution: Base: \(n=1\): LHS\(=1\), RHS\(=\frac{2}{2}=1\). ✓

Step: Assume true for \(n=k\). Then \(\sum_{r=1}^{k+1}r = \frac{k(k+1)}{2}+(k+1)=\frac{(k+1)(k+2)}{2}\). ✓

question.en: Practice: Find the four fourth roots of \(16i\) in polar form.

label.en: A system with infinitely many solutions

body.en:
Solve: \(x+z=2\), \(y=1\), \(x+y+z=3\).

Solution: The third equation is exactly the sum of the first two (\((x+z)+y=2+1=3\)) — it carries no new information.

From the first two: \(z=2-x\), \(y=1\), with \(x\) free. Infinitely many solutions: \((x,y,z)=(t,\,1,\,2-t)\) for any \(t\in\mathbb{R}\) — a whole line, exactly the "shared line" case above.
